subject: chemistry
title: Food chemistry: carbohydrates, proteins and fats

scenes.heading: Food chemistry: carbohydrates, proteins and fats
scenes.sub: The big molecules in your food, and how they break down
scenes.say: Carbohydrates, proteins and fats are the three big nutrients in food. They're large molecules built from smaller units, and digestion mostly reverses how they were built.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Each Lego click pops out a tiny piece; pulling apart needs it back
scenes.science: Condensation releases water; hydrolysis uses water to break bonds
scenes.breaks: Lego clicks together by itself, but these reactions need enzymes, and each monomer loses an H and an –OH.
scenes.say: Building these molecules is like clicking Lego together, except each click pops out a water molecule. That's condensation. Pulling them apart is hydrolysis, and each bond broken uses one water. Digestion is your body pulling the Lego apart, with enzymes doing the work.

scenes.heading: Match the bond to the food
points: n units → n − 1 bonds → n − 1 waters
scenes.say: Match the bond to the food. Sugars are joined by glycosidic bonds, proteins by peptide bonds, and fats by ester bonds. A chain of n units has n minus one links, so condensation releases n minus one water molecules.

scenes.heading: Carbohydrates
scenes.say: Glucose, fructose and galactose are simple sugars. Join two and you get a disaccharide, and every one contains glucose. Starch stores energy in plants, and glycogen in animals. We can't digest cellulose, so it passes through as fibre.

scenes.heading: Four levels of protein structure
scenes.say: Proteins have four levels of structure. Primary is the order of amino acids, held by peptide bonds. Secondary is local coiling, held by hydrogen bonds. Tertiary is the 3D shape, held by side-chain interactions. Cooking an egg denatures the shape, but doesn't break peptide bonds.

scenes.heading: Saturated vs unsaturated

right.title: Unsaturated
points: One or more cis C=C bonds

scenes.say: Saturated chains are straight, like drinking straws stacked in a box. They pack closely, so dispersion forces are strong and butter is solid. Unsaturated chains have cis double bonds that kink them, like bent straws, so they pack loosely and make liquid oils.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: What mass of water is needed to fully hydrolyse 1.00 mmol of a polypeptide of 150 amino acids?
scenes.say: One hundred and fifty amino acids have one hundred and forty-nine peptide bonds, so each chain needs one hundred and forty-nine waters. For one millimole, that's zero point one four nine moles, or two point six eight grams.
scenes.caption: 150 amino acids have 149 peptide bonds, so each chain needs 149 waters. For 1.00 mmol, that's 0.149 mol, or 2.68 g.

points: Condensation releases water; hydrolysis uses it
scenes.say: Quick recap. Condensation releases water; hydrolysis uses it. Sugars, proteins and fats have glycosidic, peptide and ester bonds. Straight chains stack, kinked chains don't. Now try the practice questions!
